name: Kachchi
confidence_why: Rohra 1966, the only full grammar of Kachchi, lists nasalization and juncture as its sole phonemic suprasegmentals and gives no word-stress rule, and Neela 1977 says the same for the Halai Bhatia sub-dialect, so with Grierson 1919 silent the record stays undetermined and no source disagrees.

catalog_quote: 2.1 Supra Segmental Phonemes: Following suprasegmental features have phonemic status in Kachi: 1. Nasalization. 2. Juncture. [p. 64] ... 2.3.3.2 Open juncture / + / The open juncture exhibits the following characteristics: (a) The vowels in the pre-junctural position are prolonged [ :]. (b) Any consonant in the pre-junctural position occurs with a sharp release and is longer than its post-junctural allophone. (c) Intensity of stress increases on the pre-junctural sound. [p. 69] ... 2.3.3.3 Terminal falling and rising junctures The terminal junctures occur in the final position of utterance. These are characterised by all features of open juncture / + / and some what longer pause. [p. 70]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not a phoneme of Kachi: the only suprasegmental phonemes recognised are nasalization and juncture (close, open/plus, terminal falling and rising). Stress is mentioned only as a phonetic correlate of open (plus) juncture — greater intensity on the last sound before the boundary, alongside vowel lengthening and sharp consonant release. The thesis gives no rule for where word stress falls; the non-contrastiveness of stress is stated by enumeration (stress omitted from the phonemic suprasegmentals), not in so many words.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Vowel length is allophonic (full length in closed monosyllables, half length elsewhere, p. 2 and p. 9); vowel allophony is conditioned by syllable type and position, never by stress (pp. 8-9).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonemic inventory (nasalization contrasts) plus utterance-level junctures; the stress remark concerns the sound immediately before an open juncture (word/morpheme boundary within an utterance), e.g. /me+thi/ 'from buffalo' vs /me thi/ 'fenugreek'. Terminal junctures carry falling vs rising pitch (statement vs question), p. 70. Description chiefly of the Mandvi (coastal) sub-dialect. Neela 1977 (Halai Bhatia sub-dialect, p. 40) independently lists the same two suprasegmental phonemes, nasalisation and juncture, with no stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Rohra 1966 describes Kachi 'chiefly based on' the Mandvi sub-dialect (coastal west Kutch: Mandvi, Mundra, Jakhau; Intro pp. II-III), distinguishing it from Bani (Jadeja/Lohana, four implosives, five nasals) and Vagdi (one implosive, three nasals) sub-dialects — all under kach1277, no separate glottocodes. Neela 1977 describes Halai Bhatia, the Kacchi sub-dialect of the Bhatia community (data from Bombay speakers), also under kach1277. Grierson's Kachchhi specimens are from Northern Cutch.

No word-stress placement rule anywhere (contents pp. i-iv, pp. 2-4, 7-9, 61-72 read from the scan; no text layer, faint typescript defeats scanned).
